Transcript block 1 (source interval 000000-000299 seconds):
[00:00:00.388] Hello everyone, welcome back to the lecture series on Python for computational problem solving. I am Nita Anjakab from the Department of Computer Science and Engineering.
[00:00:11.524] In our previous video, we looked at what computational problem solving was, and we now know that a computer or a computing device is essential for computational problem solving. So, in this video, we will look at
[00:00:28.112] the computer hardware and how it works internally.
[00:00:32.292] So the topics we would cover are the fundamental hardware components, what is digital computing, what is decimal digitization, what is information theory, binary digitization, what is an integrated circuit.
[00:00:49.156] We'll look at the binary number system and what are the terms, bits and bytes.
[00:00:55.524] So, first let's look at the fundamental hardware components. Now I know most of you know exactly what computers are, what are the components, and so on. So I'm not going to delve deep into those topics, but quickly rush through
[00:01:13.060] What the computer hardware components are and how they are connected to each other. So what is a hardware? It is the physical part of a computer system.
[00:01:24.004] So it consists of the all-important central processing unit and the memory. It also consists of some peripheral devices like the keyboard, the mouse, the printer, the monitor, etc.
[00:01:39.652] So what are the fundamental hardware components? Because we know that not every computer needs to have a printer, right? So the most fundamental hardware components are first the brain of the computer, which is your central processing unit.
[00:01:57.636] This unit is what does all the computations that we ask it to do. And the programs that run in order to tell the CPU how to compute it reside on the main memory. So all the programs reside on the main memory.
[00:02:15.588] The main memory is very close in proximity in terms of hardware to the CPU, and hence the CPU can quickly access all the information from the main memory.
[00:02:28.228] Now the main memory is volatile in nature and what that means is when the power supply is switched off, the memory is wiped clean. So it's more like a short term memory.
[00:02:40.624] If you want some information to persist for a longer time, even after your computer is turned off, we need the secondary memory.
[00:02:50.628] Which is non-volatile, and the information will remain even though there is no electricity. So examples of it are like your external hard drives, which are your magnetic drives, optical drives like your CD and DVD, and flash drives like your USB.
[00:03:11.588] So let's look at the input devices.
[00:03:16.004] And output devices, these are your mouse, keyboard, monitor, printer, and so on. So an input device technically takes input from the user, which is mostly us, and has to send it to the central processing unit. So when it does that
[00:03:33.536] How is the information going to be taken from the input device to the central processing unit? It uses something called as a bus. So we've heard the term bus even in our day-to-day lives, right? A bus is a public mode of transport.
[00:03:49.456] That takes people from point A to point B. So buses and computers does the same thing. It takes information from point A to point B.
[00:04:00.132] So there are two kinds of bus, internal buses and external buses. Internal buses are the ones which take information within the computer system, like your system bus.
[00:04:13.348] Similar to your intercity buses. Now like your interstate buses, we have external buses also that take information from outside the computer system, like from your external devices like your printers and so on to the CPU and back.
[00:04:31.236] So the layout is the brain of the computer is central, and you have all the other devices in the periphery which communicate with the CPU through these buses.
[00:04:45.988] So let's now look at what is digital computing. It basically means we need to now come up with a design that the hardware would work in a way that whatever instruction we give it should be.

Transcript block 2 (source interval 000300-000599 seconds):
[00:05:01.092] error free. So we have to ensure that your hardware is reliable.
[00:05:06.468] And in order to do so, we have to ensure that if there is no error in the hardware, only then will we get the correct result of our computation. So if there's some error, the results would also be incorrect. So what we have to do.
[00:05:23.808] is make sure that the design is simple as possible.
[00:05:27.908] So, first we have to look at what is decimal digitization, because that's what the initial design for the hardware was. So we know that the computer takes electricity as input. Now electricity is usually represented as an analog.
[00:05:44.996] information. So you can see here this is an analog sine wave, which you must have seen in your school as well. So analog signals are represented by continuous voltage. So if I want to represent information and get
[00:06:02.564] Just discrete values is where the decimal digitization came into play, where the values are represented in discrete ways in the base of 10, which is between 0 and 9. So each voltage level represented one decimal value.
[00:06:20.644] So, for example, a voltage of 4 volts would be taken as the number 4, 5 as the number 5, and no electricity as the number 0, and so on. Now this design is error prone because if there is a sudden
[00:06:36.832] spike of voltage, the information could be misinterpreted. That is when the concept of information theory was introduced by Claude Shannon, who said that all information
[00:06:50.384] Can be represented by the use of only two symbols zero and one, which is what is represented or called as binary representation. So your binary digitization is basically where each digit is represented only as zero and one.
[00:07:09.188] So we have to use a computer hardware which uses the concept of on or off. So we have an electric switch called transistors that does precisely that. So the voltage levels are now only two levels.
[00:07:24.580] Then, if there is a voltage, irrespective of what it is, would be considered as 1, and if there is no voltage, it's considered as 0.
[00:07:34.500] Now, a collection of these transistors is what we call an integrated circuit, which is the building blocks of our computer hardware. It comprises of millions or even billions of these transistors on a simple chip. Now, the pioneer of these
[00:07:51.684] concept of the integrated circuit was got in E. Moore, who said that the number of transistors that can be placed on the integrated chips would increase by double every two years. And surprisingly it still has not reached its limit.
[00:08:10.468] An interesting fact is that they say by 2030 we will have an integrated circuit or a computer that can perform all the actions that a human brain can. So we have some interesting times to look forward to in the age of computers.
[00:08:28.708] So now let's look at how information is represented. Now we are very familiar with the decimal number system.
[00:08:36.868] Where we know what is a units place, a tens place, and so on. So when we look at a number, every digit in a number is between 0 and 9, and the position of that digit determines its value.
[00:08:50.400] So let's look at how 99 is represented in decimal form. So you can see here, every column represents one power of 10.
[00:09:01.732] So tent and in computer systems the counting always starts from zero. So the rightmost column is known as your least significant column and the leftmost is the most significant column.
[00:09:16.228] So here you can see 10 to the power of 0 is 1, 10 to the power of 1 is 10, 10 to the power of 2 is 100, which is basically our units place, tens place, 100ths place, and so on. So when I represent the number 99,
[00:09:31.344] 9 in the tens place means 9 into 10, 90. 9 in the units place is 9 into 1, 9. You add it, you get 99. So how is it represented in terms of the binary number system where
[00:09:45.988] Each digit has or each column is the power of 2. So if you look at it, 2 to the power of 0, 1, 2 to the power of 1, 2, and so on. So 99 is represented as 011011.

Transcript block 3 (source interval 000600-000899 seconds):
[00:10:03.236] So each of these numbers or digits are multiplied with the power of 2. So 1 plus 2 plus 0's because these bits are turned off. 1 into 32, 32, 64 as well. So when you add all of this, you get 99.
[00:10:21.924] Now you can see that the binary representation of 99 is much larger than the decimal representation, but this is not prone to errors as much as
[00:10:34.160] the decimal digitization and gives us such a simple hardware design where you have the transistors that are just turned off or on. Based on the position, the value can be calculated. So what are each of these digits called?
[00:10:50.948] That is where we look at the concept of bits and bytes. So every binary digit is called a bit, and a collection of eight binary digits is called a byte. So let me show you one more example of converting a decimal number to a binary number.
[00:11:09.572] So when you want to convert from base 1 to base 2, you just have to divide it successively by 2. So let's convert from number 10 to binary representation. So 10 divided by 2 will give you 5 and has no remainder because it's perfectly divisible.
[00:11:28.484] 5 divided by 2 will give you 2 with the remainder 1. 2 by 2
[00:11:35.972] Value 1, remainder 0, and 1 by 2 will give you 0 with the remainder 1. So these are your binary digits. And how do we read them? We read them from bottom to top. So the one at the bottom will be the most significant bit.
[00:11:52.592] And the 0 at the top will be the least significant bit. So the binary representation of 10 is 1, 0, 1, 0. So 0 into 1 will give you 0. 1 into 2, that's 2 to the power of 1, will give you
[00:12:08.964] 2, 0 into 2 to the power of 2 will give you 0. And 1 into 2 to the power of 3, which is 8, will give you 8. 8 plus 2, 10.
[00:12:18.980] I hope you've understood how exactly the computer hardware works internally, and in the next video, I will introduce you to the computer software. We will see how the software allows us to communicate with
[00:12:32.880] the computer hardware and how this information can be given and stored. So see you in the next lecture. Thank you
